title: falarei, farei
summary: the future tense, and when people use it
intro: The future tense adds endings to the whole verb: *falar* → *falarei*. The endings are the same for -ar, -er and -ir: -ei, -ás, -á, -emos, -ão.

In conversation, Portugal usually says *vou* + verb, or the present with a time word: *Amanhã vou falar com ele* / *Amanhã falo com ele*. The future tense is more common in writing, the news, promises and formal speech.

examples.en: Tomorrow I'll speak to the director.

examples.pt: O tempo estará bom no fim de semana.
examples.en: The weather will be good at the weekend.

notes: For *ir* itself, just use the present: *Amanhã vou ao Porto*. *Vou ir* sounds wrong in Portugal.
You'll meet the future a lot in weather forecasts and the news.

drills.en: Tomorrow I'll speak to the director.
The weather will be good at the weekend.

drills.why: For *ir* itself, just the present: *vou ao Porto*. *Vou ir* sounds wrong in Portugal.

title: falaria, faria
intro: The conditional means "would". Like the future, add endings to the whole verb: -ia, -ias, -ia, -íamos, -iam. *Falaria* = I would speak.
The same three verbs shorten: *fazer* → *faria*, *dizer* → diria, *trazer* → *traria*.
In everyday Portugal the imperfeito often does this job instead: *Gostava de ir* (I'd like to go) is more common than *Gostaria de ir*, which sounds more formal.

examples.en: I'd like to make an appointment. (formal)

examples.pt: Eu no teu lugar não faria isso.
examples.en: If I were you, I wouldn't do that.

notes: Reporting what someone said about the future uses it: *Ele disse que viria* (He said he would come).
*Seria possível*…? (Would it be possible…?) is a good polite start for emails and phone calls.

drills.en: I'd like to make an appointment.
If I were you, I wouldn't do that.
He said he would come tomorrow.
She said she'd bring the wine.
I'd like to go to Sintra.
drills.why: I'd like: *gostava* (everyday) or *gostaria* (formal). *Gostarei* means "I will like".

title: será que…?
intro: The future also guesses or wonders about now: *Serão dez horas* = It must be about ten. *Onde estará a Ana*? = Where can Ana be?
*Será* que…? is a very common way to say "Do you think…?" or "I wonder if…": *Será que vai chover*?
The conditional does the same for the past: Seriam *dez horas* = It must have been about ten.

examples.en: Who can that be at this time?
He must have been about twenty.

notes: *Será*? on its own = Really? / Do you think so?

drills.en: Do you think it's going to rain?

drills.hint: ter, a guess about the past
drills.en: He must have been about twenty.
Do you think it's going to rain?
Who can that be at this time?
Do you think she's arrived yet?

drills.before: Não sei onde está a Ana.
drills.en: I don't know where Ana is. Could she be at home?
When I met him, he must have been about thirty.
drills.why: Guessing about the past: the conditional.

drills.en: Do you think the restaurant is open?
drills.why: *Será* que…? asks "do you think…?" about now or soon.

title: dir-te-ei
summary: pronouns inside the future: recognise it
intro: With the future and the conditional, a pronoun after the verb goes inside it: *dir-te-ei* (I'll tell you), *far-se-á* (it will be done), *dar-lhe-ia* (I would give him).
The pronoun sits between the verb and the ending: *dizer* → dir + te + ei. *Fazer*, *dizer* and *trazer* use their short forms.

It's formal and mostly written: the news, letters, official texts. In conversation people avoid it by using *vou* + verb (*Vou-te dizer*) or, when *não* or que comes first, by putting the pronoun in front (*Não te direi*).
notes: You need to recognise this when you read, not use it in conversation. Brazil doesn't use it at all.

drills.after: o livro, mas ele não está cá.
drills.en: I'd give him the book, but he isn't here.

drills.why: With the future, the pronoun goes inside the verb: *dir-te-ei*.
*Não* pulls the pronoun in front, so nothing is split.

drills.en: I'll tell you tomorrow. (casually, to a friend)
drills.why: Both are correct, but in conversation *vou* + verb is far more natural. *Dir-te-ei* sounds formal.
